Summarise
Singapore is recalling two Fromagerie Gillot raw milk cheeses after a possible STEC bacteria risk was found.
The recalled products are Camembert Superieur Au Lait Cru and Bertrand Pere & Fils Camembert au lait cru, both 250g, lot 232511, best before Oct 17.
SFA warned the cheese may look and smell normal but can cause serious illness, and told buyers not to eat it and to seek medical advice if worried.
AI generated
SINGAPORE –
Two raw milk cheese products from a French brand that are sold here are being recalled, because of the possible presence of a dangerous bacterium.
The two Fromagerie Gillot products are Camembert Superieur Au Lait Cru (250g) and Bertrand Pere & Fils Camembert Au Lait Cru (250g), the Singapore Food Agency (SFA) said in a media statement on Oct 9.
Both products come from the lot number 232511, and have best-before dates of Oct 17.
The European Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed ordered the recall of the products because of the possible presence of Shiga toxin-producing
Escherichia coli
(STEC).
STEC infection symptoms can include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and vomiting, with the SFA warning that food contaminated by the bacterium may not look or smell spoilt but can cause serious infections.
According to the
US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
, STEC infections can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome, which can then lead to kidney failure, permanent health problems and even death.
Cold Storage and Little Farms, which imported the products into Singapore, have been directed by the SFA to recall the products, the agency said.
Those who bought the implicated products should not consume them, SFA said, while those who have consumed the products and have concerns about their health should seek medical advice.
Consumers may contact their point of purchase for inquiries, the agency added.

SFA recalls French raw milk cheese products over presence of toxin

PHOTO:
Singapore Food Agency
PUBLISHED ON
October 09, 2026

BY
Esther Lam
European authorities have recalled Fromagerie Gillot raw milk cheese products from France due to the potential presence of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC).
The Singapore Food Agency (SFA) said on Friday (Oct 9) that as the products were brought into Singapore, it has directed the importers, Cold Storage and Little Farms, to recall the products.
The recall is ongoing, added SFA.
STEC infection can occur by consuming contaminated food, particularly raw or unpasteurised milk and its products.
Food contaminated with the toxin may not look or smell spoilt but can cause serious infections.
Symptoms of STEC infection can include diarrhoea, stomach cramps, and vomiting.
Consumers who have purchased the affected products are advised not to consume them.
Those who have already eaten the products and have concerns about their health should seek medical advice.
Consumers may also contact their point of purchase for more information.

US importer recalls 37,000 squishy toys due to ‘deadly ingestion hazard’

Published

Listen
A US-based toy importer has recalled about 37,000 squishy toys from stores nationwide due to a “deadly ingestion hazard”.
A notice on the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission’s website, which gave the recall date as Oct 1, said the two types of toys affected are Squishy Dumpling Toys and Crazy Squib Ball Toys.
These toys are manufactured in China and imported by ABC Trading, which is based in Vernon, California.
They were available at ABC Trading’s stores in Los Angeles and other stores nationwide from April to June for about US$0.41 (S$0.53) to US$1.25.
The commission said the toys had violated the mandatory product safety standard in the US, as the water beads inside them can expand larger than permitted, posing risks if ingested.
“If a water bead is ingested, it can pose ingestion, choking, and intestinal obstruction hazards inside a child’s body, resulting in severe discomfort, vomiting, dehydration and a risk of death to a child,” the commission added.
Both types of toys come in multiple translucent colours, and contain glitter and water beads.
Model 3655 of the squishy dumplings feature a cartoon face and come in a tan plastic container shaped like a bamboo steamer. These also have the words “Squishy Dumpling” printed on the front of the removable package labelling.
Meanwhile, model 3984 of the crazy squib balls are individually wrapped in a white netting, with the words “Crazy Squib Ball” and “Squeeze it! Throw it!” printed on the package labelling.
The commission has advised consumers to stop using the squishy toys immediately and contact ABC Trading for a full refund.
There have been no incidents or injuries related to the toys reported so far, it added.
According to CNBC, sales of squishy toys in the US quadrupled in 2026, reaching US$297 million (S$380.30 million) in June.
The toys’ relatively low prices and high social media appeal have been cited as the main reasons driving
their popularity.
The recall comes amid heightened scrutiny across the world over the safety of squishy toys, especially for children and young people.
In August,
nearly 20,000 illegal squishy toys were seized in Thailand
due to substandard products that may expose children to chemicals linked to cancer and other health risks.
Some squishy toys are designed to resemble food and contain added fragrance, which increase the risk of young children putting these toys in their mouth, local media The Nation had reported.
The Thai authorities had begun closely monitoring squishy toys after they became highly popular on social media, with a particular focus on TikTok and shops with high follower numbers and strong viewing figures.
Singapore has also seen a
resurgence of interest in squishy toys
, with a number of independent stores popping up over the past year.
Videos selling these toys have garnered millions of views online, with some brands also opening physical stores in places
such as
Suntec City and Chinatown.
In Singapore, stocks of popular squishy toy brand NeeDoh have run out, with the next major shipment expected in mid-October, according to NeeDoh Singapore’s official website.
“We’ve been blown away by the demand for NeeDoh this year, and we’re grateful for your support through a long wait,” the brand wrote on its website.
Singapore’s Consumer Product Safety Office (CPSO) has advised customers to choose squishy toys from reputable brands and sellers, and to avoid toys with a strong or unusual smell.
CPSO has also urged customers to check their toys regularly and to stop using any toys that are damaged, leaking, smelly or deteriorated.
“Supervise young children and never microwave or intentionally heat squishy toys,” CPSO wrote on its website.

South Korea recalls ambassador from Ukraine amid N. Korea prisoners wrangle

PHOTO: REUTERS
Published
Oct 09, 2026, 02:01 AM
Updated
Oct 09, 2026, 07:59 PM
Set as preferred source
Listen
Summarise
- South Korea will recall its ambassador to Ukraine after a row over Ukraine’s transfer of North Korean prisoners to Seoul, which Seoul says put their families in North Korea at risk.
- Ukraine urged calm and said it remains open to dialogue, while Seoul also wants an apology and says the dispute has hurt possible arms support for Kyiv.
- A separate Guardian report on fuel shipments to Russia has deepened tensions, but Seoul says refined petroleum products are not covered by its export controls and denies any breach.
AI generated
SEOUL – South Korea said on Oct 8 that it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine in response to a deepening diplomatic row over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
The two countries have been at odds since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in September
disclosed the prisoner transfer, sparking anger in Seoul,
which said it had placed the prisoners’ families in North Korea at risk.
The recall also comes days after a media report alleged that more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, had been shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August, sparking accusations that Seoul was helping to alleviate Russian fuel shortages.
“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
“The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”
Ukraine, in response, insisted that “diplomacy must prevail over emotions” in relations between the countries.
“Despite Seoul’s decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue – even if it takes time,” Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhy told reporters.
Since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, North Korea has sent troops to support Moscow’s war effort
in return for economic benefits and military technology
. South Korea’s spy agency estimated in 2025 that around 2,000 North Korean troops had been killed in the war, while a more recent assessment put the number killed or wounded at around 6,000.
Ukraine’s hopes of South Korean armament supplies have been complicated by the diplomatic row.
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on military aid to countries at war.
Seoul had already summoned Kyiv’s ambassador and threatened
unspecified
“further measures”.
President Lee Jae Myung has
demanded an official apology
over the prisoner revelation.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has called the incident a “diplomatic misunderstanding”.
More on this topic

Fuel shipment allegations
A report in Britain’s Guardian newspaper this week has threatened to deepen tensions, with allegations of fuel shipments to Russia coming as Ukraine has struck refineries deep inside Russia, while Moscow has launched intense missile attacks.
An adviser to Zelensky said this week that the alleged diesel shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies, remarks Seoul slammed as “factually incorrect” and “inappropriate”.
Seoul has been part of a coalition of countries with enhanced export controls on Russia and its ally Belarus since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
But South Korea’s Foreign Ministry on Oct 8 issued a statement saying that even if the fuel had originated in South Korea
, something it argued had not been established
, it would not breach the country’s export ban.
“Refined petroleum products
, including commercial diesel and aviation fuel, mentioned in The Guardian’s report,
are not subject to South Korea’s export controls against Russia,” it said, noting that overall exports to Moscow had more than halved since the war started.
